summary: Defines RPSL, a language operators use to describe routing policies, such as which networks they accept routes from and announce to, in the Internet Routing Registry. The policies can be detailed enough to help generate router configurations. It replaced RFC 2280.

plainLanguage.summary: A written rule book in which each network says whom it trades traffic directions with, in a form computers can read.

questions: how do import and export work in rpsl
subtitle: A text language for writing down who a network accepts routes from, announces routes to, and with what preferences.

tldr.problem: Operators need a precise, shared way to describe their routing policies so they can be kept in a common database, checked, and used to generate router configurations. The earlier language, RIPE-181, could not express some policies.
tldr.mechanism: RPSL describes policy as objects made of attribute-value lines: aut-num objects hold import, export and default rules, and route, set, router and maintainer objects supply the data they refer to. A dictionary object lets the language grow.
tldr.outcome: RPSL replaced RFC 2280, is a Proposed Standard, and has since been updated by RFC 4012 and RFC 7909.

today: RFC 2622 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 2280. It has been updated by RFC 4012 and RFC 7909, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Purpose and Design of RPSL
sections.content:
The Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) lets a network operator state routing policy at various levels of the Internet hierarchy, for example at the Autonomous System (AS) level. Policies can be given in enough detail that low-level router configurations can be generated from them, and the language is extensible.

RPSL replaces RIPE-181 (also published as RFC 1786). Operational use of RIPE-181 showed that some policies could not be expressed, and RPSL addresses those limits. The goal is a view of global routing policy kept in a single, cooperatively maintained, distributed database to improve the integrity of Internet routing.

RPSL is not a router configuration language. Configurations can be generated from an aut-num object, an inet-rtr object, and the global database of as-set, route and route-set objects. Objects are registered in the Internet Routing Registry (IRR); the registration process is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every town keeping its road rules in its own secret notebook, they all write them in one shared library in the same format. Robots can then check the rules and help build the road signs.

sections.title: Names, Types and Object Layout
sections.content:
An RPSL object is a list of attribute-value pairs, one per line, with the attribute name at column 0 followed by a colon. The attribute with the same name as the class comes first, a blank line ends the object, and continuation lines begin with a space, a tab or a plus character. Comments start at the hash character and run to the end of the line. RPSL is case insensitive and uses only ASCII. Each object is identified by a class key, and attributes are mandatory or optional, single or multiple valued.

Names are letters, digits, underscore and hyphen. Some words are reserved, such as any, from, to, accept, announce and refine. An AS number x is written ASx, an address prefix looks like 128.9.0.0/16, and dates are YYYYMMDD in UTC.

An address prefix can carry a range operator that selects its more specific prefixes. It is an error to follow one range operator with another, but an operator may be applied to a set whose members already have operators, in which case they combine.
sections.plainLanguage: Each object is a form with one fact per line, like 'name: Sam' and 'town: Oak'. A blank line means the form is finished. Special marks can mean 'this street and all the little streets branching off it'.

sections.title: Contact and Route Objects
sections.content:
The mntner class names who may create, delete and update objects. Its auth attribute chooses a scheme: NONE, MAIL-FROM, PGP-KEY or CRYPT-PW. If several are given, a request that satisfies any one is accepted as coming from the maintainer. The person and role classes hold contact details, and a role stays useful when the people performing it change. The RFC presents these classes as the common denominator of the RIPE database and tells readers to consult their own registry for the latest specification.

Each inter-AS route is registered with a route object. Its route attribute is the address prefix and its origin attribute is the AS that originates it; together they are the class key. So 128.8.0.0/16 originated by AS1 and by AS2 are two different objects.
sections.plainLanguage: A maintainer is the person with the key to the filing cabinet. A route object is a card that says 'this block of addresses is announced by this network'. Two networks can have a card for the same block and they are still different cards.

sections.title: Set Classes
sections.content:
Named sets keep policies short. There are five: as-set, route-set, rtr-set, filter-set and peering-set. Members can be listed directly, added indirectly when a member object names the set (an mbrs-by-ref attribute says which maintainers may do this, or ANY), or both. Set names start with a fixed prefix by type, and can be hierarchical, such as AS1:AS-CUSTOMERS, so that only the maintainer of the parent name can create the child.

A filter is a logical expression over routes built with AND, OR and NOT. It can match address-prefix sets, route sets, AS numbers, AS-path regular expressions written between < and >, filter-set names, and other attributes such as BGP communities. In a route set, an AS number stands for the routes it originates, and rs-any and as-any cover everything registered in the IRR.

A peering names an AS expression, optionally with router expressions on each side, using AND, OR and EXCEPT. If routers are left out, all routers of the local AS that peer with those ASes are meant.
sections.plainLanguage: A set is a team list. You can write the names on the list, or let people sign up themselves if you gave their club permission. Then a rule can say 'accept visitors from the red team' instead of naming each one.

sections.title: Import, Export and Default Policies
sections.content:
Routing policy lives in the aut-num object. An import attribute says which routes, matched by a filter, are accepted from which peerings; an export attribute says which routes are announced to which peerings. Each peering may carry an action that sets or changes route attributes, such as pref, med, community or aspath.prepend. Actions end with a semicolon and run left to right. Lower pref values are preferred, and pref is the inverse of local-pref.

Optional protocol and into parts allow policies for other protocols or injecting routes from one protocol into another, with both defaulting to BGP. The default attribute says an AS or router defaults to a peer, optionally with an action and a networks filter.

When several statements cover the same peering, the specification-order rule applies: the first one wins for the routes it covers. Import and export may also be structured with the except and refine operators, which the RFC recommends only for advanced users.
sections.plainLanguage: Import is a list of who may bring visitors into your town, and export is a list of who you tell about your roads. When two rules disagree, the one written first wins.

sections.title: The Dictionary and Extending RPSL
sections.content:
The dictionary class makes RPSL extensible. It defines routing policy attributes (rp-attributes), types and protocols. There is always a well-known dictionary named RPSL, which all tools use by default. Its initial rp-attributes are pref, med, dpa, aspath, community, next-hop and cost. Its protocol list names BGP4, OSPF, RIP, IGRP, IS-IS, STATIC, RIPng, DVMRP, PIM-DM, PIM-SM, CBT and MOSPF.

For BGP4 it defines a mandatory asno option and an optional flap_damp option. Without parameters flap damping defaults to flap_damp(1000, 2000, 750, 900, 900, 20000). Analysis tools must fetch the dictionary, and may approximate what they do not understand by treating a filter as always matching and an action as doing nothing.

Extensions are listed from most to least preferred: change the dictionary, add attributes to existing classes, add new classes, and as a last resort change attribute syntax. Extensions must keep backward compatibility, and tools should ignore attributes they do not understand.
sections.plainLanguage: The dictionary is a word list that can get new words. When routers learn new tricks, you add the word to the list and old tools just skip words they do not know.

sections.title: Aggregates, Static Routes and Routers
sections.content:
A route object becomes an aggregate when it uses attributes such as components, aggr-bndry, aggr-mtd, export-comps or holes. The origin is the AS doing the aggregation. Outside the aggregation boundary only the aggregate is exported and the more specifics are suppressed, except those named in export-comps. Aggregation may be inbound or outbound, and the inject attribute chooses which routers aggregate and under what upon condition (for example HAVE-COMPONENTS).

A route is filtered twice before export: once by the route objects and once by the AS's export policies. Overlapping aggregates are evaluated from more specific to less specific.

With upon static, inject also describes static routes, with actions such as next-hop and cost. Routers are described by the inet-rtr class, which has a DNS name, a local-as, interface addresses with mask lengths, and peer attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Aggregation is like telling far-away people only 'this whole neighborhood is over here' instead of listing every house. Neighbors who live close can still get the street-by-street map.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security story rests on the maintainer object, which controls the objects in an RPSL database. Requests from maintainers can be authenticated with the techniques named in the auth attribute.

The protocols IRRs use to exchange RPSL objects are out of scope. Several are envisioned, from interactive query and update protocols to store-and-forward ones, and the RFC expects appropriate security techniques such as IPSEC, TLS or PGP/MIME to be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the person holding the right key may change the cards in the cabinet, and the message trucks that carry the cards should be locked too.
